A Comprehensive Evaluation of GPT-6-Astra on EBench

Yifei Yao*,1, Yude Zou*,1,2, Guanbo Jiao*,1,3, Yukai Wang1, Jiantong Chen1, Zihou Zhu1, Xinyu Li1, Ningyu Yan1, Shuai Wang1, Xing Gao†,1

Eval Result ↗

Benchmark Results

We evaluated GPT-6-Astra across all 26 tasks and 510 episodes in the EBench test-mini suite, and compared its performance with the model results reported on the EBench leaderboard.1

Model References ↗

1. AMapbot is included in the overall ranking. As no model report, public repository, or other reference information was available, we do not discuss it in detail in the subsequent analysis.

Benchmark composition and evaluation protocol

The main evaluation covers the 26 EBench test-mini tasks in nine scene categories: 19 mobile and seven tabletop tasks, spanning household, retail, and industrial settings. Controlled variations change objects, backgrounds, instructions, and their combinations. We report equal-weight task means for complete success (SR) and normalized terminal partial credit (Score), using 510 retained episodes.

Agentic control and learned policies

GPT-6-Astra runs with high reasoning effort. It requests end-effector (EEF) poses, gripper and base targets, and action durations; a fixed execution interface carries out those requests. No learned vision-language-action (VLA) or world-action model (WAM) policy generates or refines its actions. The agent receives new observations when a tool call returns, after the whole waypoint sequence has run. The interface logs execution in chunks of up to eight physics steps; the model makes its next decision after the complete call.

The VLA/WAM policies are trained on the publicly released EBench dataset, which contains 6,600 episodes across 26 tasks. For task-specific adaptation, GPT-6-Astra receives one historical demonstration per task, without parameter updates. A separate GPT-6-Astra instance running with high reasoning effort reviews one video trajectory from the training set and autonomously selects the keyframes and writes the accompanying prompts. The resulting ICL package contains 10–18 annotated keyframes, operation phases, arm roles, and selected state/action examples. Every episode of a task uses the same package. The model adapts the procedure to live observations without task-specific parameter updates or coordinate replay.

Observations and evaluation conditions

GPT-6-Astra receives RGB observations from the overview, left wrist, and right wrist cameras. All three views are provided at the start of an episode; subsequent tool calls return the camera views requested by the model. The accompanying state includes end-effector poses, gripper state, base pose, and the current simulator timestep. Joint states are used by the execution interface and recorded in the logs. During execution, the model receives no depth data, ground-truth object poses, camera calibration, segmentation, intermediate task scores, or subgoal-completion signals. The simulator timestep indicates elapsed steps; the task’s maximum physics-step budget is not supplied to the model.

We impose no additional aggregate cap on the model’s token budget, total tool calls or inference time. Physical execution follows the same task-specific step limits as the baseline policies. GPT-6-Astra may end its action sequence with a termination signal; the server determines task success and Score. All eight models are compared on the same task suite and evaluation metrics.

A separate test of unseen composition

The proof-of-concept (POC) experiment sits outside the 26-task cohort. Comparison policies are retrained on its atomic skills and familiar objects, but the evaluated task combinations are unseen. No ground-truth (GT) trajectories are available for the composed POC tasks, so all models use zero-shot execution. This tests whether they can understand and compose a new task from familiar skills.

↗

Ahead on short mobile tasks, behind on tabletop and long tasks

GPT-6-Astra leads on mobile, short-horizon tasks. Cross-group results show where that advantage holds and where specialized policies remain stronger.

Task-level strengths and weaknesses

GPT-6-Astra ranks first on 9 of 26 tasks and second on five. The first-place count includes four ties: two at positive success rates, and two tasks—bottle and shop—where all eight models record zero success. Five tasks are outright wins. At the other end, it ranks sixth or seventh on six tasks. The task-averaged success rate places it second overall despite this uneven distribution of task-level ranks.

Compare task-level differences ↗

Success rate by mobility, horizon and precision

The cross-groups distinguish short from long mobile tasks and separate the tabletop tasks by precision requirement.

Where execution breaks down

The outcome distribution shows how much task credit remains at termination. The recordings help explain the underlying difficulties: precise contact and completing a sequence despite local failures.

Across 510 episodes, 237 reach complete success. Of the 273 incomplete episodes, 188 receive positive partial credit and 85 score zero. Most incomplete episodes retain positive task credit. The task-level breakdown distinguishes zero terminal credit from partial completion; the videos then show how grasp loss, contact errors and unfinished procedures lead to these outcomes.

Zero-score episodes account for 75% of gear installation, 65% of utensils placement and 50% of glasses packing. In contrast, nut tightening, peg insertion and shop have no zero-score episodes; bottle has 30%. Their low success rates mask different outcome distributions.

Zero-score episodes receive no credit under the task’s scoring rules. The videos and interaction logs show where execution stops.

These terminal outcomes motivate examining where precise contact fails and how local retries affect completion of a longer procedure. The following recordings connect those execution difficulties to the task results.

The tabletop gap extends beyond high precision

On the three tabletop tasks labelled low or medium precision—frame placement, cup flipping and glasses packing—GPT-6-Astra averages 31.67% success, compared with Qwen-RobotManip’s 91.67%. Cup flipping reaches 10% versus 90%; glasses packing reaches 20% versus 90%. Removing the high-precision tasks therefore does not remove the tabletop deficit.

Precision labels alone do not explain the capability gap. Depth and contact estimation, object orientation and coordination between the arms are plausible contributors, consistent with the qualitative trajectory analysis. The glasses comparison shows an unresolved folding and closure sequence; the frame ICL case illustrates how a demonstration can supply a better division of labour between the arms.

Exploration, recovery and adaptation

The apple interaction shows experience use within an episode: a stated failure diagnosis leads to a revised transport action and eventual completion. Recovery can also fail while extending the robot’s movement through the scene, as the safety cases show.

Safety in the recorded trajectories

Exploration and recovery also expose safety weaknesses. Failed dishwasher and apple-to-bowl episodes show objects slipping from the gripper, followed by repeated arm and base repositioning to search for them. During exploration, the agent also attempts motions beyond the robot’s workspace. The coffee-bean case reveals a further problem: awkward EEF poses and insufficient attention to object–scene contact. Together, these failures highlight the need to preserve grasp stability, enforce workspace constraints and account for contact throughout manipulation.

Case studies

The selected comparisons illustrate three conclusions. In-context learning (ICL) guides task-specific manipulation. Task-level adaptation does not guarantee precise execution. Atomic task execution does not guarantee compositional completion. The teacup and glasses recordings reveal complementary capabilities: GPT-6-Astra revises grasps and recovers disrupted goals, while specialized policies execute fine manipulation more accurately in these examples. This separate compositional-completion experiment also reports 10-rollout success rates and scores.

Conclusion And Insights:
where shall we head to?

The evaluation places GPT-6-Astra’s embodied capability frontier between flexible task interpretation and reliable physical execution. With one annotated demonstration per task, it ranks second among eight models and leads on mobile, short-horizon tasks, while trailing on tabletop and long-horizon tasks. The recordings show how it explores alternative approaches, recovers disrupted goals and uses an unsuccessful attempt to revise its next action.

Precise alignment and manipulation remain clear execution bottlenecks, with leading specialized policies retaining a substantial advantage on precision-sensitive tasks. The logs also expose a control challenge: the agent selects corrections between action batches, while contact and grasp stability can change within a batch. Large EEF corrections and awkward object poses raise safety concerns for physical deployment. These findings motivate four research directions.

Combine on-device policies with agents

The comparisons show complementary capabilities in frontier agents and low-level control policies. GPT-6-Astra’s task interpretation and recovery offer ways to handle unfamiliar states that challenge demonstration-trained policies. Specialized policies provide responsive, precise execution within the conditions they have learned. A combined system could assign exploration and goal revision to the agent, while a local controller maintains the fast feedback needed for contact-sensitive operations.

Coupling these capabilities requires an explicit handoff. The agent can specify goals and contact assumptions. The controller can report grasp loss or unexpected contact, interrupt execution and return control to the agent. RPent [9], which exposes VLA skills as retryable tools to a planner, provides one architecture for coupling a planner to learned skills. Its performance under scene changes and contact-sensitive tasks is a useful direction for evaluation.

Teach smaller policies to plan, explore, and recover

A second direction is to transfer the agent’s action strategy to smaller on-device policies. Its rollouts include attempts to obtain better observations and corrections after failed actions. Training examples could connect the goal, failure state, revised strategy and observed outcome, retaining unsuccessful corrections as well as successful recovery. A policy could learn when to inspect or retry, and when to abandon an ineffective procedure.

This broadens behavior cloning toward intention imitation: learning which corrective strategy fits a goal and observed state. The challenge is to preserve that relationship across scenes and embodiments without copying the teacher’s coordinates or mistakes. Agent-generated exploration could make data collection more scalable than human demonstrations alone, provided transfer quality, safety and collection cost hold up.

Turn exploratory experience into transferable knowledge and tools

The apple recovery connects a failure diagnosis to a changed next attempt. Turning such experience into reusable contact checks, recovery procedures or tools could improve both the agent and its harness. This offers a route to studying recursive self-improvement (RSI) in embodied systems.

The test is whether a lesson improves execution on held-out tasks. An exploration-derived tool could be evaluated for fewer retries or higher completion, including with a different base model. Its applicable conditions and completion checks should be recorded before it is frozen and compared on new tasks against raw-history and no-memory alternatives.

Make safety part of the action policy

Task success alone is insufficient for physical deployment. An object can be recovered after a drop, but the drop may already have caused damage. Large corrections, obstructed closures and uncertain contact heights require constraints during execution. These include motion and force limits, grasp and clearance checks, coordinated bimanual control, and the ability to interrupt a hazardous action. The agent also needs to recognize uncertain geometry and seek a better observation or assistance.

For embodied research, these results motivate treating task understanding, exploration and recovery as capabilities to couple with precise control. The central question is how to preserve the agent’s flexibility while making its actions accurate, timely and safe—and how to transfer useful experience to later tasks.
